transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thank you. Um, well, so I'm a student, right? I'm 21, working on my bachelor's degree, and I've been trying to apply for some internships and research positions lately. It's been a whole process, you know, gathering all the materials, getting the portfolio together, all of that. But what finally made me come in today, like the breaking point, I guess, is that I just keep... I keep turning in these applications or my research notes with these really small but just incredibly embarrassing mistakes. 

Like, for example, the other day I submitted this thing I'd been working on for weeks, and I mislabeled the date on a piece of artwork. Just completely wrong. Or I'll be filling out a form and I'll just completely skip a question. And the thing is, I honestly thought I had checked them. Like, I swear I looked over the whole document before I hit submit, and I just didn't see it. It's so frustrating because it makes me look careless, you know? Like I don't care about the opportunity, but I really do. I just... I don't know how I keep missing these things when I'm looking right at them. It's just happening so much lately that I figured I should probably talk to someone about it, because I can't keep messing up these applications over something so stupid.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about making mistakes or being judged for them, especially in situations like school or applying for opportunities?

Um, well, see, it's not really like that? It's not like I'm sitting there paralyzed with fear about being judged, you know? Like, I don't have that classic... I don't know, stage fright or whatever you want to call it when I'm applying for things. Actually, it's kind of the opposite sometimes. 

I'll feel really good about an application. Like, I'll spend all this time on my portfolio, getting all the pieces lined up, and I'll be looking at my artwork or my cover letters, and I'll think, "Wow, this is really strong, they're going to love this." So the confidence is definitely there. I'm not dreading the judgment part because I know I have the skills for the internships I'm going for, and I know my professors like my work. 

It's more just... it's the aftermath that gets me. It's not a pre-worry, if that makes sense? It's just this intense frustration after the fact when I get an email back or I look at the submitted file and realize I messed up. Like, I'm not anxious about making a mistake *while* I'm doing it, because in my head, I'm thinking, "Okay, I'm doing great, I'm checking all the boxes, everything is perfect." I genuinely believe I'm doing it right in the moment. I'm completely oblivious to the fact that I just skipped a line or wrote the wrong year. So there's no worry there, because why would I worry if I think I'm doing it perfectly? 

It's just... I guess I'm just incredibly annoyed at myself later. But no, I wouldn't say I'm, like, constantly worrying about people judging me or anything like that. I just want my stuff to reflect what I actually know and what I can actually do, and right now it's just... it's not doing that because of these tiny slip-ups. So yeah, not really a worry thing, more of a... retrospective annoyance thing.
Do you often find yourself getting distracted easily or having trouble focusing on tasks, even when you're trying your best to pay attention?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, it's actually kind of ridiculous how easily I get pulled off track. Like, I'll be sitting at my desk, right? I have this little setup in my room, I've got my laptop, my sketchbook, my coffee, everything is perfectly arranged so I can just sit down and focus on writing a cover letter or reading a paper for class. And I'll be sitting there, and I'm really trying, I swear I am. But then, I don't know, a siren will go by outside, and suddenly I'm wondering where the ambulance is going, or if there was an accident on the main road, and I'm just staring out the window. 

Or, like, I live in an apartment with a couple of roommates, and if I hear someone talking in the hallway, even if it's muffled and I can't even make out what they're saying, my brain just completely latches onto it. I'll stop what I'm doing and just listen, trying to figure out who it is or what they're talking about. And it's not even always external stuff, either. Half the time, it's my own brain. I'll be reading a paragraph, and one word will trigger a thought about this idea I had for an art exhibit, like how I could arrange the lighting or what materials I'd use, and I'll just go down this massive rabbit hole in my head. 

And the crazy part is, I won't even realize I've stopped working. I'll just be sitting there, completely lost in thought or listening to the hallway, and then suddenly I'll snap back to reality and realize, like, twenty minutes have gone by. Twenty whole minutes where I haven't read a single word or typed a single sentence. And then I have to figure out where I left off, which takes even more time, and by then I'm just so frustrated with myself because I was supposed to be getting this done. It's just... it's exhausting, honestly, having to constantly wrangle my own attention back to what I'm supposed to be doing.
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or have trouble staying seated, especially when you're trying to focus on tasks or during situations where you're expected to remain still?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I'm a particularly fidgety person, you know? Like, when I'm sitting at my desk, like I was just saying, with my laptop and my coffee, I'm usually pretty still. I'm not bouncing my leg or, like, tapping my pen incessantly or anything like that. I actually kind of hate it when people do that in the library, it's so distracting. 

But for me, physically, I'm fine just sitting there. I can sit in a lecture hall for an hour and a half and not feel like I need to jump out of my skin or pace around the room. I mean, my mind might be a million miles away, thinking about a project or wondering what I'm going to make for dinner, or, you know, analyzing the professor's tie, but my body is just sitting there perfectly normally. 

Sometimes I'll shift in my chair, but I think that's just normal, right? Like, the chairs in the science building are incredibly uncomfortable, they have this weird curve to the plastic that just digs into your lower back, so I'll kind of lean forward or cross my legs, but it's not a restless energy thing. It's just trying not to get a cramp. So yeah, I don't really have that issue of needing to move around or not being able to stay in my seat. It's really just the mental part that wanders off, not my physical body. I'm pretty content just staying put, honestly.
Looking back, did you have similar issues with attention or making mistakes in your schoolwork when you were younger, like in elementary or middle school?

Oh, wow, yeah. Going way back... um, it's funny you ask that because my mom actually kept all my old report cards. She has this big plastic bin of them at home, and it’s honestly kind of a running joke in my family now. Because if you look at, like, second grade, third grade, fourth grade... it was always the exact same comment from my teachers. Every single year. 

They would always write that I had really good ideas, you know? Like they'd say I was creative or I contributed a lot during class discussions or whatever. But then there was always this massive "but" attached to it. It was always, "he has great ideas, but he forgets to turn in his worksheets." And the frustrating thing is, I would actually do the homework! I’d sit at the kitchen table and do the math problems, but then I’d just... I don't know, shove it in my desk at school the next morning and completely forget it existed. Or I would completely lose the instructions for a project before I even made it home from the bus stop. I was just constantly missing these little details. 

It actually got so bad that my parents had to start this whole strict routine with me. Like, every single night, without fail, they had to physically open my backpack and check it. Because if they didn't, the bottom of my bag was just this absolute graveyard of crumpled-up papers and missing assignments. My dad would literally have to stand there and go through every single folder just to make sure I wasn't missing anything, because otherwise, I’d show up to class the next day completely oblivious to the fact that something was due. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing. It’s pretty much exactly what I’m doing now with my applications, just... you know, back then it was spelling worksheets instead of cover letters.
